exposure. Then in December 2020, Mass Mutual,   an insurance company founded way back in 1851,

bringing trading, custody, financing,   and other prime brokerage style services under

asset literally designed to avoid reliance   on banks. Even retirement infrastructure

within 401k plans with Micro Strategy becoming   the first announced employer to use the product.

Boring has compliance departments. Boring pays   someone to ensure billions don't disappear

building dedicated infrastructure around an asset   many still dismissed as internet funny money.

institutional machinery was being built, crypto   managed to produce another spectacular string 
of disasters. On the 9th of May 2022, TerraUSD,   an algorithmic stable coin designed to maintain 
a value of one US dollar, collapsed alongside   its sister token, Luna. Billions of dollars were 
wiped from an already falling crypto market as   the shock spread. Bitcoin dropped below $20,000

though, the dominoes started to fall. Crypto hedge   fund Three Arrows Capital went into insolveny 
proceedings in June. Lending platforms Voyager and   Celsius filed for bankruptcy in July, and for the

sheet. The crypto market was taking a beating.   Companies that looked unstoppable during the bull 
market were suddenly discovering what happened   when leverage met falling asset prices and were 
collapsing one by one. But all of this was nothing   to what came next, the collapse of FTX. By late 
2022, FTX was one of the biggest crypto exchanges   on Earth. And its founder, Sam Bankman Freed, also 
known as SPF, had become the poster boy for the   crypto industry. But in November, a liquidity 
crisis tore through the company in a matter of   days. FTX, its sister firm, Alama Research, and 
roughly 130 other affiliated companies went bust   while SPF resigned as CEO. Meanwhile, Bitcoin was 
getting absolutely hammered. After nearing $69,000   in November 2021, the FTX crisis pushed BTC below 
$16,000, more than 75% beneath its previous high.   Just like that, Bitcoin's institutional adoption 
story looked far less convincing. Crypto companies   were going bankrupt. Customers were losing 
fortunes. Regulators like the SEC were closing in.   And most of BTC's bull market gains had vanished. 
But here's where things took an unexpected turn.   If institutional adoption had simply been a 
symptom of the market euphoria of 2020 and 2021,   you'd expect Tradfi to back away when things 
started to go wrong. And while some firms   absolutely did become a lot more cautious, 
a few of the biggest names in finance were   actually moving closer. In August 2022, right 
in the middle of the crypto winter, BlackRock   partnered with Coinbase to give institutional 
users access to Bitcoin through Coinbase   Prime. That integration included trading custody 
prime brokerage and reporting. And a week later,   BlackRock went even further by launching a private 
Bitcoin trust for institutional clients in the US.   Despite the chaos, the world's largest asset 
manager wasn't about to wait for crypto markets   to look healthy again before connecting their 
institutional clients. Even so, this was a rough   period for Bitcoin. But if you've been keeping 
up with the series so far, there's a pattern   that will probably be feeling very familiar by 
now. Terror failed. Celsius failed. FTX failed.   Fortunes were wiped out. But once again, the 
Bitcoin network itself kept on chugging along   completely unfazed. It didn't file for bankruptcy 
or require some massive government bailout. Blocks   kept on coming and transactions kept settling as 
normal. 2022 had thrown the ultimate survival test   at Bitcoin and it had survived. Sure, 
BTC's price was battered and bruised,   but the network itself didn't even flinch. And 
sure enough, institutions were realizing this,   and those building infrastructure were beginning 
to separate Bitcoin from the companies collapsing   around it. And then in June 2023, things kicked up 
a gear. Black Rockck filed with the SEC to create   the Isshares Bitcoin Trust designed to hold BTC 
and give investors exposure to its price through   shares traded in the conventional financial 
system. This was huge because getting Bitcoin   into a mainstream US exchange traded product had 
become one of the industry's longestrunn battles.   People had spent roughly a decade trying to launch 
a spot Bitcoin exchange traded fund or ETF in   the United States. Yet, the SEC had repeatedly 
rejected these products, citing concerns around   fraud and manipulation in the underlying market. 
Black Rockck's application didn't guarantee   approval, but everyone had the same thought. The 
world's largest asset manager wouldn't file for   a spot Bitcoin ETF unless it expected to get the 
green light. Investors saw it as a gamecher and   BTC began recovering. For context, the SEC had 
rejected only one of Black Rockck's 575 previous   ETF applications. So, the odds were certainly 
in its favor. But something else happened that   was arguably just as important. In October 2021, 
Gayscale applied to convert its massive Bitcoin   trust into a spot Bitcoin ETF, only for the SEC to 
reject the proposal in June 2022. So, in response,   Gayscale sued the SEC. And what's crazy is that 
Gayscale actually won. In August 2023, the US   Court of Appeals ruled that the SEC had failed to 
adequately explain why it treated Gayscale spot   product differently from the Bitcoin futures 
products it had already approved. That ruling   dealt a massive blow to the SEC's anti-crypto 
position. Before long, Black Rockck, Fidelity,   Franklin Templeton, Van, Invesco, and others were 
lining up with their own products. Imagine how   bizarre that would have sounded 10 years earlier. 
Bitcoin had gone from Mount Gaus's spectacular   failure to the world's largest asset managers 
competing for permission to sell investors Bitcoin   exposure. And so after years of building a wall 
against the crypto industry, the SEC saw it come   crashing down on the 10th of January 2024. With 
no cards left to play, it approved exchange rule   changes allowing multiple spot Bitcoin products 
to trade in the US. 11 ETFs got the green light,   including offerings from Black Rockck, Fidelity, 
Gayscale, Vanek, Invesco, Franklin Templeton,   and others. The important bit though is what 
those spot Bitcoin ETFs actually do. Essentially,   each one holds Bitcoin while investors buy and 
sell shares through normal securities exchanges.   Investors don't need to open an account at 
a crypto exchange, withdraw BTC to a wallet,   or learn how to protect their own private keys. 
Bitcoin exposure could now sit alongside stocks   and traditional funds in the same brokerage 
account. A huge leap for institutional adoption.   Bitcoin finally had a rapper that fitted neatly 
into the financial system professional investors   already used. This opened the door to traditional 
investors and the money came flooding in. By the   end of May 2024, less than 5 months after 
launch, Black Rockck's Eyesshares Bitcoin   Trust had accumulated nearly $20 billion 
of assets, overtaking Gayscale to become   the world's largest Bitcoin fund. Investors had 
made one thing very clear. There was incredible   demand for accessing Bitcoin through Wall Street 
infrastructure. Notably though, the buyers of   these ETFs weren't exclusively retail traders. 
Regulatory filings showed hedge funds and other   institutional managers taking positions. And the 
number of names on Wall Street getting involved   just kept on climbing. By Q2 2024, filings showed 
that Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley had over   $600 million in combined exposure to US spot 
Bitcoin ETFs. However, they did not reveal   whether every position belonged to the banks or 
their clients. Either way though, major financial   firms that once had little reason or appetite 
to touch Bitcoin were now participating through   regulated securities products. The SEC certainly 
wasn't declaring Bitcoin safe or endorsing it.   The day it approved those 11 ETFs, Gary Gendler, 
then the SEC's chair, explicitly warned investors   about Bitcoin itself. In his words, quote, 
"While we approved the listing and trading   of certain spot Bitcoin ETP shares today, we did 
not approve or endorse Bitcoin. Investors should   remain cautious about the myriad risks associated 
with Bitcoin and products whose value is tied   to crypto. And to be clear, Wall Street hadn't 
suddenly decided Bitcoin was risk-free. However,   its clients clearly wanted exposure to it, and 
Wall Street had realized that there was money to   be made from providing that exposure. Now, by this 
point, Bitcoin's story had become almost absurd.   Go back to Bitcoin's original white paper and 
the whole idea was to create quote a purely   peer-to-peer version of electronic cash that 
would allow online payments to be sent directly   from one party to another without going through 
a financial institution. Fast forward 15 years   and those financial institutions were fighting to 
custody Bitcoin, package it into funds, and sell   it to clients. The scale of that reversal became 
ridiculous pretty quickly. Black Rockck's Bitcoin   ETF launched only in January 2024, yet ended the 
year with more than $51 billion in net assets.   Even the machinery behind the fund tells you how 
far things had come. Black Rockck sponsored it.   Coinbase held the BTC on its behalf and BNY 
Melon handled all the admin and cash custody.   Bitcoin was now plugged directly into traditional 
finance and its biggest buyers looked nothing like   its early adopters. Hedge funds, wealth managers, 
pension funds, and other institutional investors   were gaining exposure through the new ETFs using 
the same brokerage and custody infrastructure they   already relied on for traditional assets. By year 
end, Abu Dhabi's Mubadala Investment Company had   disclosed an investment of around $437 million in 
BlackRock's Bitcoin ETF. A sovereign wealth fund   was now gaining exposure to an asset once 
traded mainly by cipher punks, hobbyists,   and people using obscure online exchanges. 
Now, that doesn't mean every corporation,   pension fund, or sovereign investor suddenly loved 
Bitcoin. Plenty still wanted absolutely nothing to   do with it. But that's almost beside the point. 
Bitcoin had gone from an asset serious financial   institutions could safely ignore to one they 
desperately needed policies for accessing. And   that is probably the biggest reversal in Bitcoin's
